translationRepairs: At King Cheng’s command, the Duke of Zhou Dan raised troops against Yin, killed Wu Geng Lu Fu and Guan Shu, banished Cai Shu, and enfeoffed Kang Shu with Wu Geng’s remaining Yin people.

At King Cheng’s command, the Duke of Zhou Dan raised troops against Yin, killed Wu Geng Lu Fu and Guan Shu, banished Cai Shu, and with Wu Geng’s remaining Yin people enfeoffed Kang Shu as lord of Wei, to dwell in the former Shang ruins between the He and Qi rivers.
The idiomatic English omits 為衛君 and 居河、淇閒故商墟. The replacement restores Kang Shu’s Wei lordship and residence in the former Shang ruins between the He and Qi without adding unsupported matter.
Duke Qing ascended for twelve years and died. His son Duke Xi ascended.
Duke Qing reigned for twelve years and died. His son Duke Xi ascended.
立十二年卒 marks twelve years on the throne, not an act of ascending that lasted twelve years. “Reigned for twelve years and died” is the accurate literal rendering.
Gong Bo younger brother He had favor with Xi Hou, much gave him bribes;
Gong Bo's younger brother He had favor with Marquis Xi, who gave him many gifts;
The original is ungrammatical and leaves the giver of 賂 unclear. 有寵於釐侯，多予之賂 is He favored by Marquis Xi, who gave him many gifts; the replacement restores agent and sense.
In the fifth year of Duke Zhuang's reign, he married a Qi woman as his wife. He loved her but she had no son.
In the fifth year of Duke Zhuang's reign, he married a Qi woman as his wife. She was beautiful but had no son.
好而無子 is predicated of the Qi wife (beautiful and childless), matching the following 生子 of the Chen wife. “He loved her” invents the duke’s affection.
In Duke Zhuang's fifth year, he took a Qi woman as his wife. He loved her but she had no son.
In Duke Zhuang's fifth year, he took a Qi woman as his wife. She was beautiful but had no son.
In this sentence 好 describes the Qi woman as beautiful, not the duke’s loving her. The literal field needs the same correction as the idiomatic.
When he heard their slander, he was furious. He then sent Crown Prince Ji to Qi and ordered robbers to block him at the border and kill him. He gave the crown prince a white banner as a token.

When he heard their slander, he was furious. He then sent Crown Prince Ji to Qi and ordered robbers to block him at the border and kill him. He gave the crown prince a white banner, and told the border robbers to kill whoever held the white banner.
The original collapses 與太子白旄，而告界盜見持白旄者殺之 into a vague “token” and drops the robbers’ recognition order, which the next sentence presupposes.

Lord Qian Mou of Wei reigned for eight years. Duke Xiang of Qi, acting on the king’s command, led the feudal lords in a joint attack on Wei, restored Duke Hui of Wei, and executed the left and right ministers.

Lord Qian Mou of Wei reigned for eight years. Duke Xiang of Qi, acting on the king’s command, led the feudal lords in a joint attack on Wei, restored Duke Hui of Wei, and executed the left and right princes.
左右公子 are the left and right princes, already so rendered in the preceding unit. “Ministers” is a rank error.

Initially, when the Di killed Duke Yi, the people of Wei pitied him and thought of again installing a descendant of Duke Xuan’s deceased former crown prince Ji. Ji’s son had also died, so they installed his younger brother Shen, making him Duke Dai.

Initially, when the Di killed Duke Yi, the people of Wei pitied him and thought of again installing a descendant of Duke Xuan’s deceased former crown prince Ji. Ji’s son had also died, and Shou, who had died in Ji’s place, also had no son.
This unit ends at 子壽又無子. The original invents Shen’s installation as Duke Dai (from later sentences) and omits that Shou, who died in Ji’s place, also had no son.
Crown Prince Ji had two half-brothers from the same mother: one was called Qian Mou. Qian Mou once replaced Duke Hui as lord, and after eight years again left;
Crown Prince Ji had two younger brothers from the same mother: one was called Qian Mou. Qian Mou once replaced Duke Hui as lord, and after eight years again left;
同母弟 are younger brothers by the same mother. “Half-brothers” wrongly implies they did not share a father; these sons of Duke Xuan are uterine younger brothers, not half-brothers.
The grand officer Yuan Tiao attacked Duke Cheng, and Duke Cheng fled.
The grand officer Yuan Xuan attacked Duke Cheng, and Duke Cheng fled.
元咺 is Yuan Xuan (咺, xuān). Tiao is a false reading of the given name.
Grand officer Yuan Tiao attacked Duke Cheng, and Duke Cheng fled.
Grand officer Yuan Xuan attacked Duke Cheng, and Duke Cheng fled.
The same name 元咺 must be Yuan Xuan in the literal field as well.
Then Zhou pleaded on his behalf with Duke Wen of Jin. He finally re-entered Wei, executed Yuan Tiao, and Wei lord Xia fled.
Then Zhou pleaded on his behalf with Duke Wen of Jin. He finally re-entered Wei, executed Yuan Xuan, and Wei lord Xia fled.
誅元咺 is the execution of Yuan Xuan, not Yuan Tiao.
Then Zhou requested on his behalf to Duke Wen of Jin. He finally entered Wei, and executed Yuan Tiao. Wei lord Xia fled.
Then Zhou requested on his behalf to Duke Wen of Jin. He finally entered Wei, and executed Yuan Xuan. Wei lord Xia fled.
The literal likewise misreads 元咺 as Tiao; Xuan is the correct English form.
In the twenty-sixth year, Bing Chan of Qi assassinated their lord Duke Yi.
In the twenty-sixth year, Bing Chu of Qi assassinated their lord Duke Yi.
邴歜 is Bing Chu (歜, chù). Chan does not match the character.
In the twenty-sixth year, Qi's Bing Chan assassinated their lord Duke Yi.
In the twenty-sixth year, Qi's Bing Chu assassinated their lord Duke Yi.
The literal field repeats the same false reading of 歜 as Chan.
The concubine, with favor, hated Cao to the duke. The duke also whipped Cao three hundred times.
The concubine used her favor to speak ill of Cao to the duke. The duke also whipped Cao three hundred times.
惡曹於公 is to speak ill of Cao before the duke, not “hated Cao to the duke.” The replacement restores the slander construction.
The day grew late without summons, and they went to shoot geese in the park.
The day grew late without summons, and he went to shoot geese in the park.
The silent subject of 而去射鴻於囿 is Duke Xian; 二子從之 in the next unit shows the ministers followed him. “They went” misassigns the hunt.
The two sons followed him. The duke did not remove his hunting clothes and spoke with them.
The two men followed him. The duke did not remove his hunting clothes and spoke with them.
二子 here resumes Sun Wenzi and Ning Huizi, not biological sons of the duke.
The two sons were angered and went to Su.
The two men were angered and went to Su.
二子 continues the same two ministers. Rendering them as “sons” is a kinship error.
Sun Wen Zi's son often served the duke drinks and made Shi Cao sing the final stanza of clever words."
Sun Wenzi's son often served the duke drinks and made Shi Cao sing the final stanza of 'Clever Words'.
The stray closing quote is a corruption, and 巧言 is the poem title, not generic clever words.
Duke Shangqiu took the throne and enfeoffed Sun Wenzi Linfu at Su.
Duke Shang, Qiu, took the throne and enfeoffed Sun Wenzi Linfu at Su.
殤公秋 is Duke Shang, personal name Qiu, not a fused toponym-like Shangqiu. The preceding unit already separates the posthumous title and the given name.
In the twelfth year, initially Kong Yuwen Zi married the crown prince Kuai Kui's sister, and she gave birth to Pei.
In the twelfth year—this had happened earlier—Kong Yu, posthumously Kong Wenzi, married the crown prince Kuai Kui's sister, and she gave birth to Kui.
悝 is Kui, not Pei, and 孔圉文子 is Kong Yu, posthumously Wenzi, not a fused Yuwen. 初 marks the marriage and birth as prior to the twelfth-year narrative.
In the twelfth year, initially Kong Yuwen Zi took the crown prince Kuai Kui's sister and gave birth to Pei.
In the twelfth year, originally Kong Yu Wenzi took the crown prince Kuai Kui's sister to wife, and she gave birth to Kui.
生悝 is the sister’s giving birth, not Kong Yu’s. The original also misreads 悝 as Pei.
Hun Liangfu, an attendant of the Kong clan, was handsome and capable. After Kong Wenzi died, Liangfu had relations with Pei’s mother.
Hun Liangfu, an attendant of the Kong clan, was handsome. After Kong Wenzi died, Liangfu had illicit relations with Kui's mother.
美好 describes appearance, not “capable,” 通於 is illicit intercourse, and 悝 is Kui. The replacement corrects all three without adding matter.
The Kong clan's elder Luan Ning asked him, and he called the marriage concubine to tell him.
The Kong clan's elder Luan Ning asked them, and they identified themselves as in-law concubines in reply.
稱姻妾以告 means the disguised pair identified themselves as marital concubines, not that someone summoned a concubine. 問之 refers to the two who had just arrived.
After the meal, Pei’s mother took a ge spear and went first. The crown prince followed with five armored men, carrying Xi with him.
After the meal, Kui's mother took a ge-halberd and went first. The crown prince and five armored men followed, with a sacrificial boar borne along.
輿猳 is a boar borne along for the covenant, not a person named Xi. 悝母 is Kui’s mother.
He summoned guards and harnessed the chariot. They passed around wine and roast, and escorted Duke Chu Zhe as he fled to Lu.
Shao Hu harnessed the chariot. They passed around wine and roast, and escorted Duke Chu Zhe as he fled to Lu.
召護 is the personal name Shao Hu, the driver, not a command to summon guards.
He summoned protection and harnessed the chariot. They circulated wine and drank roast, served Duke Chu Zhe who fled to Lu.
Shao Hu drove the chariot. They circulated the wine-cup and ate the roast, and served Duke Chu Zhe, who fled to Lu.
召護 names the charioteer; 食炙 is eating the roast, not drinking it. The original misreads both the name and the verb.
Zi Lu said, "Why does the crown prince employ Kong Pei?
Zi Lu said, "Why does the crown prince employ Kong Kui?

孔悝 is Kong Kui, not Kong Pei, but 焉用 is “employ/what use in using,” and the original’s “employ” is accurate. Only the personal name needs repair; keep the rest of the human wording, including the unclosed quotation that continues in the next unit.
Kong Pei finally installed Crown Prince Kuaikui, who became Duke Zhuang.
Kong Kui finally installed Crown Prince Kuai Kui, who became Duke Zhuang.
孔悝 is Kong Kui. Splitting 蒯聵 as Kuai Kui matches the established English name in this chapter.
適 is the same man named Prince Shi (公子適) in the previous sentence. Rendering him as Di here splits one person into two English names.
Wei changed course and installed the heir lord’s younger brother, who became Lord Yuan.
Wei then installed Lord Si’s younger brother, who became Lord Yuan.
嗣君 is the ruler Lord Si, not a generic heir-lord, and 更立 is installing a replacement, not “changing course.”

Grand Historian said: I read hereditary houses speak, arrived at Xuan Gong crown prince because wife seen executed, younger brother Shou contended death to yield each other, this with Jin crown prince Shen Sheng dared not clarify Li Ji transgression same, both disliked injure father intention.

The Grand Historian said: I read the hereditary-house accounts, and when I reached Duke Xuan's crown prince who was executed because of his wife, and the younger brother Shou who contended over dying in mutual yielding, this was the same as Jin's crown prince Shen Sheng not daring to make clear Li Ji's fault; both disliked injuring their father's will.
The current literal is not English. The replacement restores the comparison of Duke Xuan’s crown prince and Shou with Jin’s Shen Sheng, and the shared refusal to injure their fathers’ will.
Yet finally died death, how sad!
Yet in the end they died. How sad it is!
卒死亡 is that they died in the end, not a doubled “died death.” The silent subject is the princes just named.
